title: Isolator Transmissibility Explorer
description: Three calculation challenges (two attempts, ±5%): the learner types the transmissibility of an undamped isolator for a stated fan speed and static deflection, then sees the operating point and their answer on the T versus frequency-ratio curve; afterwards Explore mode varies speed and deflection with live readouts of f, fn, r, T and percent isolation.

educational.audience: Adult professional development: new application engineers, sales staff, representatives and facilities staff
learningObjectives: The learner will calculate the transmissibility of an undamped isolator from the fan speed and the isolator's static deflection, to within 5% of the model value.

accessibility.notes: Plot container has role=img and an aria-label; every plotted value is also in a polite live text readout with a ▲/▼ region label; the model point (square) and the learner's answer (open diamond) differ in shape and are labelled; verdicts announced through FP.announce; Enter checks and moves on; native range and select controls in Explore mode.

rules: Answers within ±5% of the unrounded model T are correct; two attempts per challenge.
When T > 1 the readout shows 'amplified ×T' instead of a negative percentage.
When |r - 1| < 0.05 the readout shows 'at or near resonance' and the plotted T is capped at 10.
Display values are rounded to 3 significant figures.
Mastery is 3 of 3 on the first attempt.
assumptions: Undamped single-degree-of-freedom isolator on a rigid floor; fan speeds are illustrative.
limitations: Real isolators have damping, which limits T at resonance; a flexible roof or mezzanine is not rigid.

sources: FanPedia: The Fan & Blower Encyclopedia (Twin City Fan), p. 134 (isolator deflections), https://tcf.com/fanpedia/
Standard undamped single-degree-of-freedom model; fan speeds illustrative.

pedagogical.teachingStrategy: Commit a calculated value before the curve is revealed, then explore the parameter space
keyQuestions: What fraction of the fan's force gets through a 1 in spring at 1170 RPM?
Why does the same pad isolate a fast fan and amplify a slow one?
What happens to the natural frequency when the deflection doubles?
commonMisconceptions: An isolator that works on one fan works on any fan.
Doubling deflection halves the natural frequency.
assessmentOpportunities: First-attempt score shown as 'First-attempt score: n of 3'; mastery is 3 of 3 on the first attempt.
